P. Morgan. results.content:
energy transfer technology. In 2007, wireless power transfer shocked the world again, the research team headed by Professor Marin Soljacic of MIT proposed strongly coupled magnetic resonance (SCMR), and they were able to transfer 60 watts wirelessly with ~40% efficiency over distances in excess of 2 meters . Subsequently, Intel and Qualcomm also demosntrated their wireless power transfer systems, which indicated that this novel technology would soon appear in our daily life. [...] Version Notes

Order Reprints

## Abstract

Strongly coupled magnetic resonance (SCMR), proposed by researchers at MIT in 2007, attracted the world’s attention by virtue of its mid-range, non-radiative and high-efficiency power transfer. In this paper, current developments and research progress in the SCMR area are presented. Advantages of SCMR are analyzed by comparing it with the other wireless power transfer (WPT) technologies, and different analytic principles of SCMR are elaborated in depth and further compared. The hot research spots, including system architectures, frequency splitting phenomena, impedance matching and optimization designs are classified and elaborated. Finally, current research directions and development trends of SCMR are discussed.

Nikola Tesla first discovered resonant coupling during his pioneering experiments in wireless power transfer around the turn of the 20th century, but the possibilities of using resonant coupling to increase transmission range has only recently been explored. In 2007 a team led by Marin Soljačić at MIT used two coupled tuned circuits each made of a 25 cm self-resonant coil of wire at 10 MHz to achieve the transmission of 60 W of power over a distance of 2 meters (6.6 ft) (8 times the coil diameter) at around 40% efficiency. In 2007, a team led by Marin Soljačić at MIT used a dual resonance transmitter with a 25 cm diameter secondary tuned to 10 MHz to transfer 60 W of power to a similar dual resonance receiver over a distance of 2 meters (6.6 ft) (eight times the transmitter coil diameter) at around 40% efficiency. [...] Further information: Tesla coil § Resonant transformer

Resonant inductive coupling (electrodynamic coupling, strongly coupled magnetic resonance) is a form of inductive coupling in which power is transferred by magnetic fields (B, green) between two resonant circuits (tuned circuits), one in the transmitter and one in the receiver. Each resonant circuit consists of a coil of wire connected to a capacitor, or a self-resonant coil or other resonator with internal capacitance. results.title: Schumann resonances - Wikipedia
results.content:
The real Earth–ionosphere waveguide is not a perfect electromagnetic resonant cavity. Losses due to finite ionosphere electrical conductivity lower the propagation speed of electromagnetic signals in the cavity, resulting in a resonance frequency that is lower than would be expected in an ideal case, and the observed peaks are wide. In addition, there are a number of horizontal asymmetries—day-night difference in the height of the ionosphere, latitudinal changes in the Earth's magnetic field, sudden ionospheric disturbances, polar cap absorption, variation in the Earth radius of ± 11 km from equator to geographic poles, etc. that produce other effects in the Schumann resonance power spectra.[citation needed]

## Measurements [...] In the normal mode descriptions of Schumann resonances, the fundamental mode is a standing wave in the Earth–ionosphere cavity with a wavelength equal to the circumference of the Earth. The lowest-frequency mode has the highest intensity, and the frequency of all modes can vary slightly owing to solar-induced perturbations to the ionosphere (which compress the upper wall of the closed cavity)[citation needed] amongst other factors. The higher resonance modes are spaced at approximately 6.5 Hz intervals (as may be seen by feeding numbers into the formula), a characteristic attributed to the atmosphere's spherical geometry. calc.custom_code:
import sympy as sp

# Can receivers draw power "for free"? Write the energy balance and solve it.
P_in, eta, N, p_home = sp.symbols("P_in eta N p_home", positive=True)
balance = sp.Eq(eta * P_in, N * p_home)          # what arrives = what is used
P_needed = sp.solve(balance, P_in)[0]             # -> N*p_home/eta

homes = 1_000_000        # one million homes (assumption, for scale)
per_home_w = 1_000       # 1 kW average draw per home (assumption)
eff = 0.5                # a generous 50% end-to-end link efficiency (assumption)
need = P_needed.subs({N: homes, p_home: per_home_w, eta: eff})

claimed_input_w = 0      # the "free energy" version: nothing extra at the tower
result = {
    "metrics": {
        "formula": str(P_needed),
        "tower_power_needed_w": float(need),
        "tower_power_needed_gw": float(need) / 1e9,
        "claimed_extra_input_w": claimed_input_w,
    },
    "summary": f"Serving {homes:,} homes at {per_home_w} W needs {float(need)/1e9:.1f} GW at the tower, "
               "even at a generous 50% link. 'Free' means 0 W in, which the balance forbids.",
    "violates_energy_conservation": claimed_input_w < float(need),
    "suggested_verdict": "BREAKS PHYSICS",
}

claims.archive_query: energy delivered to receiving circuits is supplied by the generator at the transmitting station

explanations.C1: This part is real. Even a deliberately simple two-coil model gives about {efficiency_at_claimed_distance_pct:.0f}% at {claimed_distance_m:g} m, and MIT measured about 40% at 2 m in 2007 (S7). But the curve collapses fast: below 1% by about {distance_where_efficiency_drops_below_1pct_m} m.
explanations.C2: Not forbidden, but the medium leaks. The Earth-ionosphere cavity rings with peaks about 20% wide (S11), which means Q of about {q_factor:.0f}: stored energy drains in about {energy_ring_down_s:.2f} s, about {ring_down_in_cycles:.1f} oscillation cycles. Nobody has shown a low-loss global path, so most of the station's power would be lost in the cavity rather than delivered.
explanations.C3: This is the myth part. Serving a million homes at 1 kW needs about {tower_power_needed_gw:.1f} GW going in at the tower even with a generous 50% link. Power out can never exceed power in, so 'free' wireless electricity breaks conservation of energy.

concept.name: Tesla Shelf
concept.pitch: A bookshelf that powers everything sitting on or near it, no cables, no pads.
concept.who_its_for: Small offices, cafes and classrooms with a tangle of phones, lamps and sensors.
concept.how_it_works: A tuned coil hidden in the shelf drives matching resonant receivers in phone cases, lamps and IoT sensors within about a metre, the same physics MIT demonstrated in 2007 (S7).
concept.honest_limits: About 10 W per device at half a metre, and efficiency halves by about 0.75 m (see the spec sheet). At full power the exposure screen says keep people roughly 0.85 m from the coil's axis, or run below about 0.6 W. It will never power a house across town.

The simpler two-electron reaction to produce hydrogen at the cathode can be electrocatalyzed with almost no overpotential by platinum, or in theory a hydrogenase enzyme. If other, less effective, materials are used for the cathode (e.g. graphite), large overpotentials will appear.

[edit]

The electrolysis of water in standard conditions requires a theoretical minimum of 237 kJ of electrical energy input to dissociate each mole of water, which is the standard Gibbs free energy of formation of water. calc.custom_code:
import sympy as sp

# Thermodynamic floor for splitting water, from Gibbs energy and Faraday's law.
dG = sp.Rational(237130)          # J/mol, Gibbs energy of formation of liquid water (S2, S3)
F = sp.Rational(96485)            # C/mol, Faraday constant (S3)
n = 2                             # electrons per H2O molecule split
E_min = dG / (n * F)              # minimum cell voltage
mol_per_litre = sp.Rational(1000, 18)
energy_per_litre_mj = dG * mol_per_litre / 10**6

claim = "splits water below the 237 kJ/mol thermodynamic minimum"
result = {
    "metrics": {
        "minimum_cell_voltage_v": round(float(E_min), 3),
        "minimum_energy_kj_per_mol": float(dG) / 1000,
        "minimum_energy_mj_per_litre": round(float(energy_per_litre_mj), 2),
        "court_expert_finding": "conventional electrolysis (S1)",
    },
    "summary": f"No cell can split water below {float(E_min):.3f} V, i.e. "
               f"{float(energy_per_litre_mj):.1f} MJ per litre. Court experts found Meyer's cell "

In the 1950s, Warren Rice attempted to recreate Tesla's experiments, but he did not perform these early tests on a pump built strictly in line with Tesla's patented design (it, among other things, was not a Tesla multiple staged turbine nor did it possess Tesla's nozzle). Rice's experimental single-stage system's working fluid was air. Rice's test turbines, as published in early reports, produced an overall measured efficiency of 36–41% for a single stage. Higher efficiency would be expected if designed as originally proposed by Tesla. [...] The device functions as a pump if a similar set of disks and a housing with an involute shape (versus circular for the turbine) are used. In this configuration, a motor is attached to the shaft. The fluid enters near the center, is energized by the disks, and exits at the periphery. The Tesla turbine does not use friction in the conventional sense, rather using adhesion (the Coandă effect) and viscosity instead. It uses the boundary-layer effect on the disc blades.

[edit]

The turbine was patented by Nikola Tesla on October 21, 1913, which was his 100th patent.

For the new turbine it is possible to bring the 1.063 kg flywheel up to about 40 rpm with 15 good breaths through the inlet hose, then sustain rotation by easier breaths, and, for a while, not pass out. With the pump style volute it was possible to get the flywheel to move, but not to sustain rotations by breath alone. calc.custom_code:
# Same electricity, different turbines: how much more fuel would a Tesla turbine burn?
steam_turbine_eff = 0.90      # large steam turbines: "over 90% in practice" (S3)
tesla_turbine_eff = 0.41      # best single-stage measurement, Rice (S3)
plant_output_mw = 500         # a mid-size power plant (assumption, for scale)

shaft_energy_in_steam = plant_output_mw / steam_turbine_eff
shaft_energy_in_tesla = plant_output_mw / tesla_turbine_eff
extra_fuel = shaft_energy_in_tesla / shaft_energy_in_steam - 1

result = {
    "metrics": {
        "steam_turbine_eff_pct": steam_turbine_eff * 100,
        "tesla_turbine_eff_pct": tesla_turbine_eff * 100,
        "steam_energy_needed_mw": round(shaft_energy_in_steam, 1),
        "tesla_energy_needed_mw": round(shaft_energy_in_tesla, 1),
        "extra_fuel_pct": round(extra_fuel * 100, 1),
    },
    "summary": f"A Tesla turbine at today's measured efficiency would need about "
               f"{extra_fuel*100:.0f}% more steam (fuel) for the same 500 MW.",
    "violates_energy_conservation": False,
    "suggested_verdict": "MISSING PIECE",
}

explanations.C1: The principle is sound and has been built many times. At {disc_gap_mm:g} mm gaps and 10,000 rpm the boundary layer is about {boundary_layer_mm:.2f} mm thick, so the discs really do drag the fluid. Measured single-stage efficiency is {measured_efficiency_pct}% (S3).
explanations.C2: Nothing forbids high efficiency, but nobody has measured it: Tesla projected up to 97%, tests report around 40% (S2, S3). That leaves {unexplained_gap_pct_points:.0f} percentage points that no published test has reproduced.
explanations.C3: At today's measured efficiency a Tesla turbine would burn about {extra_fuel_pct:.0f}% more fuel than a large steam turbine for the same power. That's why it lost the market, not a conspiracy.

concept.name: DiscFlow Pump
concept.pitch: A bladeless pump that doesn't clog and is gentle on whatever it moves.
concept.who_its_for: Small fish and shrimp farms, and workshops pumping dirty or abrasive water.
concept.how_it_works: Stacked smooth discs drag the water by boundary-layer friction, so there are no blades to snag debris or bruise fish; the same physics as Tesla's 1913 turbine run in reverse (S3, S4).
concept.honest_limits: Hydraulic efficiency is around 20-30% (S4), well below a good centrifugal pump. It's worth it only where clogging, shear or noise matter more than electricity cost.
